title: Atomisation and HTML: My Honest Journey Using AI to Plan Lessons Part 2
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele offers two honest updates on his AI-assisted planning journey: a pedagogical correction and a technical breakthrough. Revisiting Kris Boulton's work, he distinguishes "small steps" (breaking a process into a sequence of actions, teaching how but not why) from true Atomisation (breaking a cognitive routine into its constituent conceptual atoms), warning that conflating the two is a "lethal mutation." On the technical side, he abandons hours of Google Slides design in favor of a Webpage Creator Gem that generates bespoke HTML pages, models, mini-whiteboard sequences, and worksheets, precisely targeting each atom, while deliberately excluding the responsive, human "Do Now" from automation.
points: Atomisation and "small steps" are not synonyms; treating them as such is, in Boulton's phrase, a "lethal mutation."
Small steps break a process into a sequence of actions (teaching how); atomisation breaks a cognitive routine into conceptual atoms, revealing structure and relationships (teaching why).
Emanuele's earlier Lesson Planning Gem sometimes generated small steps rather than true atomisation, prompting a dedicated Atomisation Gem.
A new Webpage Creator Gem replaces hours of slide-building, generating I-Do/We-Do/You-Do models, mini-whiteboard sequences, and worksheets tailored to the exact atom.
The "Do Now" is deliberately excluded from automation because it depends on responsive, human judgment about the specific class in front of you.
quotes: In the rush to make learning accessible, it is easy to confuse atomisation with small steps. As Boulton points out, treating them as synonyms is a “lethal mutation.

Small Steps usually mean breaking a process down into a sequence of actions. While this makes the task easier to complete, it often fails to reveal the underlying mathematical structure, relationships, or concepts. It teaches how, but not why.
Atomisation, by contrast, involves breaking a cognitive routine down into its constituent atoms. Each “atom” is a specific concept, fact, or another cognitive routine
When you atomise a concept down, you often realise the specific questions you need simply don’t exist.
Previously, I would spend hours designing Google Slides to fill this gap. I have stopped doing that.
the Do Now must be a dynamic, human process. It depends entirely on the specific class in front of you, what they struggled with yesterday, what they have forgotten from last month
